romania.title: Cercetătorii au descoperit că inima are un „sistem electric de rezervă”. Tratamentul aritmiilor cardiace s-ar putea schimba
romania.summary: Oamenii de știință au descoperit că inima dispune de un mecanism suplimentar prin care impulsurile electrice sunt transmise între celulele musculare. Cercetarea, realizată de specialiști de la Virginia Tech și Ohio State University, din Statele Unite, ar putea contribui la explicarea unor tulburări de ritm cardiac, inclusiv fibrilația atrială. Descoperirea sugerează că inima poate transmite semnale electrice chiar și atunci când anumite conexiuni dintre celule sunt slăbite, dar mecanismul nu a fost încă demonstrat într-o inimă umană în funcțiune.

medical.title: Genomic work helps find treatment for rare blood disorder
medical.summary: Sisters with a rare blood condition are the first patients to receive a repurposed drug to treat it, after a team of doctors and cardiovascular scientists used genomic sequencing to identify the drug's target.

medical.title: When is it time to treat obesity? An expert explains it's not just a lack of willpower
medical.summary: If you're trying to figure out how to treat obesity, the choices can feel overwhelming. Diet plans, weight-loss surgery, newer pills and weekly injections all promise results, and it's hard to know when and where to start.

medical.title: Novel platform reveals new metabolic targets for cancer treatment
medical.summary: Cancer cells are hungry beasts. To fuel growth and division, tumors rewire a cell's metabolism, diverting nutrients into the energy and raw materials they need to survive. But not all cancers have the same metabolic needs, and a new study reveals how different cancer-causing mutations can shape metabolism even within the same organ.

medical.title: An engineered 'glue' for aged eggs could prevent premature chromosome separation
Oral nutrition supplement interventions show short-term benefits in patient outcomes at low cost for older adults
medical.summary: A systematic review published in the journal Value in Health by Amarsinh Desai, Ph.D., Olivia M. Dong, Ph.D., and colleagues examines the health and economic effects of oral nutrition supplements in older adults, most with or at risk of malnutrition. The researchers found that oral nutrition supplement use, often as part of broader nutrition interventions, was generally associated with modest short-term improvements in health outcomes and was cost-effective or cost-saving, with economic benefits largely driven by reductions in health care resource utilization, such as fewer hospitalizations.

medical.title: A protein that teaches cells to tolerate DNA damage points to a new vulnerability in cancer
medical.summary: Cancer begins in DNA, which is why everything about this well-known molecule is extensively studied at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO). For instance, what exactly happens when DNA is duplicated? Every time a cell divides into two daughter cells, its DNA is copied. Researchers at CNIO and Stanford University have now uncovered a new aspect of this complex process, which has been studied for decades but still holds many surprises.

medical.title: Experimental drug shows promise in overcoming treatment resistance in aggressive acute myeloid leukemia
medical.summary: Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that an experimental drug may help overcome one of the major challenges in treating an aggressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), known as FLT3-positive AML. In laboratory and animal studies, the drug, called PHI-101, was effective against leukemia cells carrying genetic mutations that cause resistance to existing FLT3-targeted therapies.

medical.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

medical.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

medical.title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
medical.summary: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

medical.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
medical.summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

medical.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
medical.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

science.title: Protein redesign boosts DNA insertion activity and reveals how molecular machinery selects targets
science.summary: Genome engineering is exciting, given its vast potential to treat and even cure diseases, but it is still a largely uncharted biomedical innovation. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital recently uncovered the mechanisms involved in precisely integrating DNA into a target genomic location using CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs). By studying type I-F3 CAST, the researchers unveiled structural findings that explain how this CAST family achieves successful DNA integration at precise target sites and offer insights for future genomic engineering approaches. The results were published in Nature.

science.title: Scientists discover quasar formed within a mere 630 million years of the Big Bang, setting a record
science.summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

science.title: Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds
science.summary: Between roughly 9,000 and 4,000 B.C., artists in ancient Scandinavia painstakingly carved large, sometimes life-size images of elk, reindeer, bears and other creatures into rock faces teetering on the edge of fjords, rivers and lakes. But their meaning has long been debated.

science.title: Sensory deterrents aren't a 'one-size-fits-all' solution for sharks and rays
science.summary: A study on how select species of rays and sharks respond to sensory deterrents has reinforced why there isn't a one-size-fits-all solution to prevent fisheries bycatch.

science.title: Many buyers willing to pay more to know where their food comes from
science.summary: New research from Curtin University reveals many Australians are prepared to pay more for food when they know where it comes from and how animals are treated, despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures.

science.title: Mathematics fact fluency interventions for students with mathematics difficulties
science.summary: Associate professor Jonté Myers knows that developing fluency with mathematics facts is key to mathematics proficiency. However, many students struggle to develop these foundational skills.

science.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
science.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

science.title: 'King tide' waves batter California coast, soaking San Francisco
science.summary: Massive waves carried on king tides battered California's coast Wednesday, prompting evacuations and soaking San Francisco, but sparing feared mass disruptions to Thanksgiving holiday travel.

science.title: Some miniature Cas12m proteins can cut DNA after all
science.summary: An international research group led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga, Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura and Professor Osamu Nureki from the University of Tokyo has demonstrated for the first time that some Cas12m proteins do have an active state capable of cutting, or "cleaving," DNA. The team also clarified the structural differences between the active and inactive variations.

science.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
science.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-held, lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

science.title: Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations
science.summary: Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.

science.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
science.summary: New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

science.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
science.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

science.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
science.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

science.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
science.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

science.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
science.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

science.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
science.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

science.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
science.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

science.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
science.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

science.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
science.summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
environment.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
environment.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
environment.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: Cercetătorii au descoperit că inima are un „sistem electric de rezervă”. Tratamentul aritmiilor cardiace s-ar putea schimba
mix_items.summary: Oamenii de știință au descoperit că inima dispune de un mecanism suplimentar prin care impulsurile electrice sunt transmise între celulele musculare. Cercetarea, realizată de specialiști de la Virginia Tech și Ohio State University, din Statele Unite, ar putea contribui la explicarea unor tulburări de ritm cardiac, inclusiv fibrilația atrială. Descoperirea sugerează că inima poate transmite semnale electrice chiar și atunci când anumite conexiuni dintre celule sunt slăbite, dar mecanismul nu a fost încă demonstrat într-o inimă umană în funcțiune.

mix_items.title: Novel platform reveals new metabolic targets for cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: Cancer cells are hungry beasts. To fuel growth and division, tumors rewire a cell's metabolism, diverting nutrients into the energy and raw materials they need to survive. But not all cancers have the same metabolic needs, and a new study reveals how different cancer-causing mutations can shape metabolism even within the same organ.

mix_items.title: An engineered 'glue' for aged eggs could prevent premature chromosome separation
Oral nutrition supplement interventions show short-term benefits in patient outcomes at low cost for older adults
mix_items.summary: A systematic review published in the journal Value in Health by Amarsinh Desai, Ph.D., Olivia M. Dong, Ph.D., and colleagues examines the health and economic effects of oral nutrition supplements in older adults, most with or at risk of malnutrition. The researchers found that oral nutrition supplement use, often as part of broader nutrition interventions, was generally associated with modest short-term improvements in health outcomes and was cost-effective or cost-saving, with economic benefits largely driven by reductions in health care resource utilization, such as fewer hospitalizations.

mix_items.title: A protein that teaches cells to tolerate DNA damage points to a new vulnerability in cancer
mix_items.summary: Cancer begins in DNA, which is why everything about this well-known molecule is extensively studied at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO). For instance, what exactly happens when DNA is duplicated? Every time a cell divides into two daughter cells, its DNA is copied. Researchers at CNIO and Stanford University have now uncovered a new aspect of this complex process, which has been studied for decades but still holds many surprises.

mix_items.title: Experimental drug shows promise in overcoming treatment resistance in aggressive acute myeloid leukemia
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that an experimental drug may help overcome one of the major challenges in treating an aggressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), known as FLT3-positive AML. In laboratory and animal studies, the drug, called PHI-101, was effective against leukemia cells carrying genetic mutations that cause resistance to existing FLT3-targeted therapies.

mix_items.title: Protein redesign boosts DNA insertion activity and reveals how molecular machinery selects targets
mix_items.summary: Genome engineering is exciting, given its vast potential to treat and even cure diseases, but it is still a largely uncharted biomedical innovation. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital recently uncovered the mechanisms involved in precisely integrating DNA into a target genomic location using CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs). By studying type I-F3 CAST, the researchers unveiled structural findings that explain how this CAST family achieves successful DNA integration at precise target sites and offer insights for future genomic engineering approaches. The results were published in Nature.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover quasar formed within a mere 630 million years of the Big Bang, setting a record
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

mix_items.title: Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds
mix_items.summary: Between roughly 9,000 and 4,000 B.C., artists in ancient Scandinavia painstakingly carved large, sometimes life-size images of elk, reindeer, bears and other creatures into rock faces teetering on the edge of fjords, rivers and lakes. But their meaning has long been debated.

mix_items.title: Sensory deterrents aren't a 'one-size-fits-all' solution for sharks and rays
mix_items.summary: A study on how select species of rays and sharks respond to sensory deterrents has reinforced why there isn't a one-size-fits-all solution to prevent fisheries bycatch.

mix_items.title: Many buyers willing to pay more to know where their food comes from
mix_items.summary: New research from Curtin University reveals many Australians are prepared to pay more for food when they know where it comes from and how animals are treated, despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures.

mix_items.title: Mathematics fact fluency interventions for students with mathematics difficulties
mix_items.summary: Associate professor Jonté Myers knows that developing fluency with mathematics facts is key to mathematics proficiency. However, many students struggle to develop these foundational skills.

mix_items.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
mix_items.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

mix_items.title: 'King tide' waves batter California coast, soaking San Francisco
mix_items.summary: Massive waves carried on king tides battered California's coast Wednesday, prompting evacuations and soaking San Francisco, but sparing feared mass disruptions to Thanksgiving holiday travel.

mix_items.title: Some miniature Cas12m proteins can cut DNA after all
mix_items.summary: An international research group led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga, Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura and Professor Osamu Nureki from the University of Tokyo has demonstrated for the first time that some Cas12m proteins do have an active state capable of cutting, or "cleaving," DNA. The team also clarified the structural differences between the active and inactive variations.

mix_items.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
mix_items.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-held, lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

mix_items.title: Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations
mix_items.summary: Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.

mix_items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
mix_items.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

mix_items.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

mix_items.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
mix_items.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

mix_items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
mix_items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

mix_items.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
mix_items.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

mix_items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
mix_items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

mix_items.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
mix_items.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

mix_items.title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
mix_items.summary: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

mix_items.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
mix_items.summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

mix_items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
mix_items.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
